s-quran--the-quran-was-preserved-through.html: The Quran reached us through mass oral memorisation and early written codices at the same time, each checking the other, so a corruption in one would have been caught by the other.

1. P1A text is reliably preserved when it is fixed early and transmitted by many independent people who can check each other.
  2. P2The Quran was memorised in full by many Companions during the Prophet's lifetime, written down under his supervision, gathered into one codex within two years of his death (Abu Bakr, c. 632-634), and copied into a standard edition sent to every major city within about twenty years (Uthman, c. 650).
  3. P3Every later generation recited the whole text publicly (in prayer, especially Ramadan) in front of thousands, and its manuscripts are checked against living memorisers to this day.
  4. ∴The Quran meets the conditions of a reliably preserved text far better than any other scripture of antiquity.

The written text was not an afterthought. The Prophet ﷺ had scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mu'awiya write each revelation as it came, and the Companions recited it in their prayers every day. When many reciters were killed at the Battle of Yamama, Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the written fragments into one book. Zayd collected the Quran from written fragments and from memorisers (Bukhari 4986); later scholars such as Ibn Hajar explain that he required two witnesses for each verse.

Under Uthman (c. 650), disputes over regional pronunciations led to an official copy in the Qurayshi dialect. It was made from Abu Bakr's codex (kept with Hafsa) and sent to Kufa, Basra, Damascus and Mecca, and the private copies that differed were burned. The Companions agreed to this, including Ali, who said: "Had I been in his place I would have done the same."

The modern academic picture backs this up. Angelika Neuwirth, writing in the Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an, notes that newly found fragments support an early fixed text and that the "revisionist" theories of a late, evolving Quran have failed. Seyfeddin Kara (The Integrity of the Qur'an) concludes the codex can be dated with certainty to before Umar's death (23/644).

Source Seyfeddin Kara, The Integrity of the Qur'an: the codification dates to the earliest period

The radiocarbon-dated Birmingham folios (568-645 CE), the Sana'a lower text and the Hijazi codices such as BnF Arabe 328 show a text that is, in the portions preserved, very close to today's Quran. The Sana'a lower text does contain variants, which scholars debate. Corpus Coranicum lets anyone compare any verse across these early manuscripts. Dated Arabic inscriptions from the same years show the script in use: a tombstone in Cyprus is dated Ramadan 29 AH.

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ

15:9

إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُ وَقُرْآنَهُ

75:17

"Oral transmission is unreliable."

For ordinary stories, yes. But the Quran was a fixed text recited word for word, with set rhythm and rhyme, and corrected publicly in congregational prayer. A memoriser who changes a word is corrected by the people behind him. That is the opposite of a game of whispers. And the written channel ran alongside it from the start.

"Uthman burned copies, so he must have destroyed the real Quran."

What he destroyed were private copies with dialectal spellings, personal glosses or a different surah order. The text itself was checked against Abu Bakr's codex and against the memorisers still alive, who included the senior reciters. No Companion is reported to have accused Uthman of adding or removing a verse, although Ibn Mas'ud objected to the burning of his own codex and to the choice of Zayd. If a verse had been removed, his enemies would have said so.

"There are variant readings (qira'at), so there are different Qurans."

See the next argument. The readings were taught by the Prophet himself and are part of the revelation, not later copying errors.

Your opponent says

“Uthman burned the other Qurans, so we only have his version, not Muhammad's.”

Uthman copied from Abu Bakr's codex, compiled within two years of the Prophet's death from written pieces confirmed by memorisers, and the senior reciters were alive to check it. Not one Companion, including his political enemies, accused him of altering a verse; Ali said he would have done the same.

The Quran was memorised by thousands, written under the Prophet's supervision, gathered within two years of his death and standardised within twenty. Today's text matches the first-century manuscripts. Few ancient scriptures combine a continuous oral recitation tradition with manuscripts radiocarbon-dated to within decades of the founder.

s-quran--non-muslim-scholars-concede-the.html: Even scholars hostile or indifferent to Islam admit that the Quran we have is the one Muhammad ﷺ taught.

1. P1A concession from a hostile or neutral witness carries more weight than praise from an insider.
  2. P2A long line of Western orientalists, many of them critical of Islam, state that the Quran is unaltered.
  3. ∴The preservation of the Quran is accepted across the scholarly spectrum; it is not just a Muslim claim.

• William Muir, a missionary-minded critic of the Prophet: "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
  • Stanley Lane-Poole: there is no doubt of the Quran's authenticity, and it has come down unchanged.
  • Kenneth Cragg (Anglican bishop): there is no room for doubt that what we have is essentially what Muhammad taught.
  • John Burton: the Quran we have is the text "as it was arranged and approved by the Prophet".
  • Neal Robinson, H.A.R. Gibb, R.V.C. Bodley, C.C. Torrey, Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri make similar statements .

Source William Muir on the purity of the Quranic text

"These are old orientalists; modern scholars are more sceptical."

The trend is the opposite. The revisionist school of the 1970s (Wansbrough, Crone and Cook) argued for a late Quran, but the manuscript finds since then (Sana'a, Birmingham, Tübingen) have pushed the text back to the Prophet's generation. Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, accept that most of the Quran goes back to Muhammad's lifetime, while still describing a text that developed within his community.

Your opponent says

“Modern scholars like Wansbrough and Crone said the Quran was compiled centuries later.”

Their theories predate the manuscript evidence. The Birmingham folios are radiocarbon-dated to 568-645 CE, and Sana'a and Paris codices show the same text in the first century. Even critical scholars like Sinai now say the late-Quran thesis has failed.

From Muir to Neuwirth, scholars who have no stake in defending Islam increasingly accept that the Quran text goes back to Muhammad's generation. The manuscript discoveries of the last forty years have only made that consensus stronger.

s-quran--the-qira-at-are-revealed-readin.html: The canonical readings of the Quran go back to the Prophet ﷺ himself, differ in only a small fraction of words, and complement each other in meaning.

1. P1A copying error is accidental, unsupported by a chain to the source, and usually makes worse sense.
  2. P2Each canonical reading needs a sound chain to the Prophet (many scholars require mass transmission), must fit the Uthmanic consonantal outline, and must be correct Arabic. The Prophet explicitly approved different readings.
  3. ∴The readings are deliberate, authorised variations within the revealed text, not corruption.

In Bukhari 2419, Umar heard Hisham ibn Hakim recite Surah al-Furqan differently from how he himself had learned it. He brought Hisham to the Prophet ﷺ, who had both recite and said of each: "It was revealed like this." He added that the Quran was revealed in seven ahruf (modes), "so recite whichever is easy for you".

Ibn Mujahid's survey found that only about 700 of the Quran's roughly 77,000 words differ between the readings, and almost all of those differences are in vowels or verb forms. They usually add meaning rather than contradict it:

  • Maliki/Maaliki yawm al-din (1:4): "King of" and "Master of" the Day of Judgement. Both are true of Allah.
  • Nunshiruha/nunshizuha (2:259): "We raise them" and "We assemble them". Both describe the bones of the man raised to life.

Ibn Taymiyya compares each reading to a separate verse (Majmu' al-Fatawa 13/391).

إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ أُنْزِلَ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ فَاقْرَءُوا مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنْهُ

Bukhari 2419

"If the text was perfectly preserved, why are there differences at all?"

Because the differences were revealed. Preservation means the text is exactly as it was given, and it was given with these readings. The Bible's variants are the opposite case: they come from scribes changing the text after the fact, as Metzger and Ehrman document (see Corruption of the Bible).

Your opponent says

“Hafs and Warsh are different Qurans, so the Quran wasn't preserved.”

They are two authorised readings. The Prophet approved different recitations (the seven ahruf), and the canonical qira'at are held by scholars to preserve authorised recitations; how exactly the ahruf relate to the qira'at is discussed among scholars. They share the same consonantal text, differing in about 1% of words, mostly vowels, with complementary meanings like 'King' and 'Master' of the Day of Judgement. Preservation means preserved as revealed, and it was revealed with these readings.
The readings are authorised by the Prophet, transmitted by mass chains, limited to about 1% of words, and they enrich the meaning. Calling them "errors" misunderstands what they are.

s-quran--the-missing-verses-reports-answ.html: The reports critics cite (the goat, Ubayy's two extra surahs, Ibn Mas'ud's codex, the "valley of gold" and the "200 verses of al-Ahzab") are either weak, or describe abrogation that the Quran itself announces (2:106), or concern supplications rather than surahs.

1. P1A claim of loss needs authentic evidence that a verse the Prophet ﷺ wanted kept in the recited Quran disappeared.
  2. P2Each report either has a weak chain, describes a verse whose recitation the Prophet himself withdrew (naskh al-tilawa), or describes text the Companions themselves did not count as Quran.
  3. ∴None of these reports shows that anything Allah intended for the final Quran was lost.

• The goat that ate the page (Ibn Majah 1944). The "goat" detail comes only through Muhammad ibn Ishaq, a mudallis whose solitary additions are weak (graded weak by al-Arna'ut). The verses mentioned, stoning and the suckling verse, had their recitation abrogated during the Prophet's lifetime while some rulings remained. That is why Imam Malik said the suckling text "is not acted upon".
    • Ibn Hazm: the Companions memorised the Quran, so "a sheep eating a paper changes nothing".
    • Al-Baqillani: it is absurd to think the Companions relied on one sheet under a bed.
  • Ubayy's "two extra surahs" (al-Khal' and al-Hafd). These are the qunut supplication, which Ubayy wrote in his personal codex as a du'a (al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 3142). The reports about them have chain gaps of two or three generations. Ubayy himself dictated to Zayd during Uthman's compilation (Kanz al-'Ummal 4789), so he agreed with the final text.
  • Ibn Mas'ud's codex "of 111 surahs". No physical codex of his exists. Ibn al-Nadim saw several so-called Ibn Mas'ud codices and none of them agreed with each other. Ibn Mas'ud is reported not to have written the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his personal codex (Musnad Ahmad; see Bukhari 4977), and scholars explain this as his view that they were protective prayers or that they needed no writing. Three of the canonical readings ('Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i) run through his students, and these include al-Fatiha and the Mu'awwidhatayn. At most, he did not write the short protective surahs in his personal notebook because everyone knew them.
  • “If the son of Adam had a valley of gold…” Ibn Abbas said he did not know whether it was from the Quran. Ubayy said they thought it was until Surah al-Takathur was revealed (Bukhari 6437, 6438, 6440), so it is a hadith or an abrogated wording.
  • "Al-Ahzab was as long as al-Baqara." The reports in Musnad Ahmad run through Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad and 'Asim, whose memory was criticised, so they are weak.

مَا نَنسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنسِهَا نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِّنْهَا أَوْ مِثْلِهَا

2:106

"Abrogation is just a way of explaining away lost verses."

Abrogation is announced in the Quran itself: "Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better or similar" (2:106; also 87:6-7). A verse withdrawn by the Prophet ﷺ in his lifetime was not lost; it was removed by the same authority that revealed it. Loss would mean that something meant to stay disappeared, and no authentic report says that.

Your opponent says

“Aisha said a goat ate the verses of stoning, so parts of the Quran are lost.”

The goat detail comes only through Ibn Ishaq, whose solitary additions are weak. The verse's recitation was abrogated in the Prophet's lifetime, as 2:106 allows. And the Companions had memorised the Quran; Ibn Hazm said a sheep eating a page changes nothing.
Each "missing verse" report is either weakly transmitted, describes abrogation the Quran itself announces, or concerns a supplication. None shows that anything meant to remain in the Quran was lost.

s-hadith--hadith-were-written-down-in-th.html: Written hadith collections existed in the Companions' and Successors' generation, and their contents match the later canonical books almost word for word.

1. P1If hadith were invented in the 2nd-3rd centuries, first-century collections should either not exist or differ greatly from Bukhari and Muslim.
  2. P2First-century collections such as the Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih exist, and their texts are almost identical to the same hadith in Ahmad, Bukhari and Muslim.
  3. ∴The canonical collections faithfully preserve earlier material; the hadith were not invented later.

The Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih. Hammam was a student of Abu Hurayra (d. 58 AH) and wrote down 138 hadith from him in the mid-first century. The full text survives in manuscript (the Damascus MS) and is quoted whole in Musnad Ahmad. Ninety-eight of its hadith are in Bukhari or Muslim. R. Marston Speight compared the versions (Der Islam 77, 2000). He found "almost complete identity" and "practically no sign of careless or deceptive practices".

Source Arabic Literature to the End of the Umayyad Period on the Sahifa of Hammam

Source Study conclusion: the Sahifa's material is uniformly prophetic hadith, preserved with its chains

Writing was permitted early. "Do not write from me anything except the Quran" (Muslim 3004) was an early precaution so that the two would not be mixed. The Prophet ﷺ later permitted writing:

  • "Write for Abu Shah" (Bukhari 2434).
  • He told 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr to write, "for only truth comes out of it" (Abu Dawud 3646).
  • Ali kept a written sahifa (Muslim 1370).
  • Letters were sent out with written rulings, such as 'Amr ibn Hazm's letter and Abu Bakr's book of zakat.

وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانتَهُوا

59:7

"Goldziher and Schacht proved hadith were forged to support later legal positions."

Their method assumed a hadith was fake unless proven otherwise and looked at late legal texts. Harald Motzki studied the earlier Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq (d. 211 AH) systematically. He concluded that its reports from figures like 'Ata' and Ibn Abbas were genuinely transmitted. He wrote that rejecting hadith as a source for the first century, a view "to which I myself adhered", deprives history of an important source.

Source Motzki: the prophetic hadith in the Musannaf are not later fabrications

Source Motzki's conclusion after studying the Musannaf

"The isnad system is arbitrary; critics just graded narrators as they liked."

Scott C. Lucas compared the grades given by three early critics (Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Ma'in and Ibn Hanbal), who worked independently. They agree on 80-87% of the narrators they all graded. Arbitrary grading would not produce that level of agreement; a consistent method does.

Source Scott C. Lucas: the 78 men graded by all three critics

Source Lucas on the agreement between Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Hanbal

Your opponent says

“Hadith were collected 200-250 years after Muhammad, so they're unreliable hearsay.”

Bukhari compiled from earlier written collections. The Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih, written by a student of Abu Hurayra, survives and matches Musnad Ahmad almost word for word, and Motzki dated material in 'Abd al-Razzaq's Musannaf to the first century.

First-century written collections exist and match the canonical books; the scholar who studied the earliest material most closely abandoned the forgery thesis; and the early critics graded narrators with measurable consistency. The hadith are a preserved source.

s-history--the-argument-from-historical-.html: An unlettered man in 7th-century Arabia stated facts about ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia that were unknown in his time, absent from the Bible and Jewish lore, and only confirmed by modern archaeology. The best explanation is a source beyond him.

1. P1If someone with no access to a body of knowledge accurately reports details from it, details unknown to his contemporaries and absent from every source available to him, the best explanation is that he received them from a source with that knowledge.
  2. P2The Quran contains such details: the title "king" for Joseph's ruler but "Pharaoh" for Moses' ruler, Pharaoh's baked-brick tower, the Egyptian motif of heaven and earth weeping for the dead, a deified Pharaoh who still had gods of his own, and Abraham's rejection of the Mesopotamian astral triad.
  3. P3The Prophet ﷺ could not read, never went to Egypt, had no Arabic Bible, and the Bible and midrash either lack these details or get them wrong. Hieroglyphs were unreadable until Champollion (1822) and cuneiform until the mid-1800s.
  4. ∴The best explanation is that the Quran comes from the One who knows the unseen.

Egyptian sources became readable only recently. The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 and Champollion deciphered it in 1822. Before 1822, nobody could correctly read Egyptian royal titles or funerary texts, although medieval Arabic authors such as Ibn Wahshiyya attempted to decipher hieroglyphs. Cuneiform was cracked by Rawlinson and others in the 1850s. Several details below have been argued to fit evidence uncovered after those decipherments.

"He could have heard these from Jews or Christians in Arabia."

The test is simple: the details are not in the Jewish or Christian sources. On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus), the Bible differs from the Quran. You cannot copy a correction from the text you are correcting.

"These are lucky guesses."

One lucky guess is possible. A pattern across many independent details, each matching evidence found only centuries later, is not. And in each case the Quran departs from the obvious source, which is exactly where a guesser would follow it.

Your opponent says

“Muhammad just picked up Bible stories from travelling Christians and Jews.”

Then he'd reproduce the Bible's details, including its errors. Instead the Quran uses 'king' for Joseph's ruler, describes baked brick in Moses' Egypt, and names the Mesopotamian astral triad: details absent from the Bible and confirmed only by modern archaeology.

The Quran repeatedly corrects the Bible on ancient Near Eastern details that nobody could check until the 19th century. An unlettered man copying from the Bible would reproduce its errors, not fix them.

s-history--king-in-joseph-s-time-pharaoh.html: The Quran calls Joseph's ruler al-malik (the king) and Moses' ruler Fir'awn (Pharaoh). This fits the Egyptian use of "pharaoh" as a royal title from the New Kingdom, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler. Many Egyptologists call the biblical usage retrospective.

1. P1The word "pharaoh" (per-aa, "great house") was used for the king himself only from the New Kingdom (c. 1550 BCE), especially from Thutmose III onwards.
  2. P2Joseph lived well before that, plausibly under the Hyksos, while Moses lived in the New Kingdom.
  3. P3The Bible uses "Pharaoh" for the rulers of Abraham's and Joseph's eras (Gen 12, Gen 41). The Quran uses "king" for Joseph's ruler (12:43, 50, 54) and "Pharaoh" only for Moses'.
  4. ∴The Quran is precise where the Bible is anachronistic.

Source British Museum Dictionary of Ancient Egypt (Shaw & Nicholson): before the New Kingdom the use of "pharaoh" is strictly anachronistic

Alan Gardiner (Egyptian Grammar, p.75) and W.V. Davies (Egyptian Hieroglyphs, p.45) give the same dating. Maurice Bucaille notes that nobody at the time of revelation could have known this distinction.

Source Scholars note the biblical use of "pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler is an anachronism

وَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ إِنِّي أَرَىٰ سَبْعَ بَقَرَاتٍ سِمَانٍ

12:43

"'King' and 'Pharaoh' are synonyms, so this proves nothing."

If they were interchangeable, we would expect the Quran to mix them, as it uses other synonyms freely. Instead it never calls Joseph's ruler Pharaoh, in a surah of over 100 verses, and it calls Moses' ruler Pharaoh 74 times. That consistency tracks the historical change exactly.

"Maybe the Bible uses 'Pharaoh' as a modern-style label, like calling all Roman rulers 'Caesar'."

That is precisely the anachronism. The Quran avoids it.

Your opponent says

“'Pharaoh' was used loosely for any Egyptian king, so the Bible isn't wrong.”

As a title, 'Pharaoh' (per-aa, 'great house') was applied to the king only from the New Kingdom, about 1550 BCE. Joseph lived earlier. The Quran consistently uses 'king' for Joseph's ruler and 'Pharaoh' for Moses' ruler, which is exactly right.
The Bible calls every Egyptian ruler "Pharaoh"; Egyptology shows the title began in the New Kingdom. The Quran uses "king" for Joseph's era and "Pharaoh" for Moses', consistently.

s-history--pharaoh-s-tower-of-baked-bric.html: Pharaoh orders Haman to "kindle fire upon clay" to build a tower (28:38). Baked brick was rare in Egypt, though it is attested in Middle Kingdom Nubian forts and in New Kingdom Thebes, and Petrie found Ramesside examples at Nebesheh. Many place Moses in the Ramesside era, but this is debated.

1. P1Egyptian building was overwhelmingly stone and sun-dried mud brick; fired brick was unusual.
  2. P2Petrie found burnt brick in the Ramesside Delta (Nebesheh) in a tomb bearing Ramesside names.
  3. P3The Quran describes exactly this technique in Moses' time and pairs it with the royal ambition to "reach the ways of the heavens", which echoes the Pyramid Texts' ladder for the king to ascend to the sky.
  4. ∴The Quran's detail fits the Egyptian evidence for that period.
Source The Quran's description: baked clay (kiln-fired brick) and a high structure "to reach the ways of the heavens"

فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يَا هَامَانُ عَلَى الطِّينِ فَاجْعَل لِّي صَرْحًا

28:38

"The Bible's Tower of Babel had baked bricks, so the Quran just moved the story to Egypt."

The Babel story is set in Mesopotamia, where fired brick was normal. The Quran puts it in Egypt, where it was rare, and in an era where Egyptology finds it. A copyist relocating a Babel story would not know to choose that era.

Your opponent says

“Haman was Persian, from the book of Esther; the Quran mixed up the stories.”

Haman in the Quran is Pharaoh's official in charge of building, a role, not Esther's Persian vizier. Names recur across cultures, and the detail of firing clay for a tower fits the Ramesside Delta, where Petrie found baked brick.
"Kindle fire upon clay" describes fired brick, which Petrie found appearing in the Ramesside Delta, the time of Moses.

s-history--abraham-and-the-astral-triad.html: The Quran has Abraham reject a star, then the moon, then the sun (6:75-79). This is precisely the top triad of Mesopotamian religion: Venus (Ishtar), Moon (Sin) and Sun (Shamash).

1. P1In Mesopotamia from the 3rd millennium onward the Moon-god Sin, Sun-god Shamash and Ishtar (Venus) were prominent, and they appear together on seals and on Kassite kudurru stones (later 2nd millennium BCE).
  2. P2The Bible only says Abraham's fathers "served other gods" (Josh 24:2). Jewish legends give different lists: fire, water and earth (Apocalypse of Abraham 7) or "the stars" in the plural (Jubilees 12).
  3. P3The Quran names exactly the triad, in the observational order of an evening sky: Venus as the evening star that sets soon after sunset, then the moon, then the sun.
  4. ∴The Quran's sequence star, moon, sun is consistent with the astral worship of Mesopotamia and Harran.

Source Some scholars regard dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC as sustainable, though many scholars doubt he is a historical figure.

Ibn Kathir already explained the kawkab as Venus, centuries before anyone could read a kudurru inscription.

فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ رَأَىٰ كَوْكَبًا ۖ قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّي ۖ فَلَمَّا أَفَلَ قَالَ لَا أُحِبُّ الْآفِلِينَ

6:76

Your opponent says

“The star-moon-sun story is just a rabbinic legend Muhammad heard.”

The rabbinic versions list different objects and orders. The Quran names exactly the Mesopotamian top triad, Venus, the moon and the sun (Ishtar, Sin, Shamash), as shown on kudurru boundary stones, which no one in Arabia could read.
The Bible says "other gods"; Jewish legends get the list wrong. The Quran names the star, the moon and the sun, which is exactly the Mesopotamian astral triad found on kudurru stones.

s-history--more-egyptian-details-the-bib.html: Several smaller details in the Quran's Moses story fit Egyptian evidence better than the biblical account does.

1. P1A cumulative case is built from many independent details that each fit the evidence.
  2. P2The details below each fit Egyptian evidence, and each is either absent from the Bible or contradicted by it.
  3. ∴Together they strengthen the inference that the Quran's source knew Egypt.

• "Neither heaven nor earth wept for them" (44:29). Egyptian funerary texts promise the dead king that "the sky weeps for thee, the earth trembles" (Pyramid Text Utterance 553) and "heaven and earth weep for thee" (Songs of Isis and Nephthys). The Quran inverts the formula for the drowned Pharaoh, a motif only readable after 1822.
  • A deified Pharaoh who has gods (79:24 with 7:127). Critics call it a contradiction that Pharaoh says "I am your lord most high" while his chiefs speak of "your gods". New Kingdom kings like Ramesses II were worshipped as divine while themselves worshipping Amun, Ra and Ptah. The Quran describes exactly that.
  • The rivers beneath Pharaoh (43:51). In the Quran, Pharaoh boasts of owning the Nile's channels, which is realistic royal propaganda. In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it", a creator claim.
  • A small band (26:54). Pharaoh calls the Israelites "a small band". The Bible has 600,000 men leaving Egypt, a number archaeology has found no trace of. The Quran gives no number, and its "small band" is the more plausible picture.

Source The Bible has Pharaoh claim to have made the Nile (Ezek 29:3); the Quran has him claim to own the rivers (43:51)

  • The Samiri (20:85-97). Critics allege an anachronism with "Samaria". The Samiri's identity is debated; some proposals derive the name from Hebrew shomer or from an Egyptian term (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary, a dated source). He led the Israelites to a calf cult reminiscent of the Apis bull.

Source E.A. Wallis Budge, An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary, vol. II: shemer, "stranger, foreigner"

  • Pharaoh's body preserved as a sign (10:92). New Kingdom royal mummies survive. The Bible says nothing about Pharaoh's body.
  • Haman. Christians say Haman belongs to the Persian court of Esther. But the Quran's Haman is an Egyptian official, and the name is argued by some to be an Egyptian title (Muhammad Asad, Hamen/Hmn), a view Silverstein rejects in JSAI 34, where he derives the Quranic Haman from the Book of Esther.

Source The Egyptian background of the name Haman

"The Quran borrowed Haman from Esther and got the era wrong."

This assumes there can be only one person with a name or title. The Quran never links its Haman to Persia, to Esther or to Mordecai. And the Egyptian evidence gives a real setting for an official with that title.

Your opponent says

“These details are too small to prove anything.”

Each is small, but each goes against the Bible and matches Egyptian evidence. A copier doesn't keep correcting his source in the direction of archaeology he can't access.
Weeping heaven and earth, a god-king with gods, rivers he owns rather than made, a small band of Israelites, a foreign "shemer": each detail fits Egypt and departs from the Bible.

s-history--muhammad-is-attested-by-outsi.html: Non-Muslim sources from the 630s-660s describe a prophet among the Arabs who preached the God of Abraham, forbade wine and fornication, and whose followers conquered Persia and Syria. That is the Muhammad of Islamic history, not a later invention.

1. P1If Muhammad were a later legend, early non-Muslim witnesses should be silent or describe someone different.
  2. P2Within a few decades of 632, Greek, Syriac and Armenian Christian sources, and then coins and inscriptions, name him and describe his message and movement in terms that match the Islamic sources.
  3. ∴Muhammad ﷺ is a firmly attested historical figure who taught what Islam says he taught.

• Doctrina Jacobi (634): "a prophet has appeared among the Saracens".
  • Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640): mentions "the Arabs of Muhammad" (Mhmt, which some read as a title).
  • The Khuzistan Chronicle (c. 660): the Arabs led by MHMD conquered Persia.
  • Sebeos, Armenian bishop (c. 660s): Muhammad was a merchant who preached the God of Abraham, knew the Law of Moses, and forbade carrion, wine, lying and fornication.

Source The Armenian History attributed to Sebeos (Liverpool, Translated Texts for Historians)

  • Isho'yahb III, Catholicos of the Church of the East (c. 650s): the Arabs "are not only no enemy to Christianity, but are even praisers of our faith".
  • Physical evidence:
    • The Arab-Sasanian coins of Bishapur (66 AH) and later issues read "Muhammad is the messenger of God" in Pahlavi.
    • Abd al-Malik's dinars of the 70s AH carry the shahada.
    • The Hisma inscription, dated about 80 AH, reads "O God, bless Muhammad the Prophet".

Source An early inscription: "O God, send blessings upon Muhammad the Prophet"

  • The Syriac chronicle of the mid-8th century says Muhammad traded to Palestine.
  • Chinese sources: the Tang account and Du Huan (750s) describe the Arab religion, including prayer and a ban on wine .

Source Mid-8th-century Syriac chronicle on Muhammad's trading journeys

"The Islamic sources are too late; Muhammad might be a myth."

The revisionists of the 1970s argued this, but they did not survive the evidence. Robert Hoyland (Seeing Islam as Others Saw It) collects dozens of non-Muslim witnesses within 150 years in six languages. Sinai's verdict above is now widely held.

Your opponent says

“Muhammad might be a later invention; the Islamic sources are late.”

The Doctrina Jacobi (634) mentions a prophet among the Saracens; Sebeos (c. 660) describes him preaching the God of Abraham and forbidding wine and fornication; Isho'yahb III describes the Arabs. Sinai concludes a late-7th-century invention is improbable.

Within thirty years of his death, Byzantine, Syriac and Armenian Christians were describing Muhammad ﷺ as a prophet of the God of Abraham who forbade wine and fornication. Coins and inscriptions confirm it, and Islamic history is corroborated by its rivals.

s-history--the-quran-s-stories-are-not-c.html: Critics say the stories of Dhul-Qarnayn, the Sleepers of the Cave and Abraham smashing the idols were borrowed from Syriac or rabbinic legends. In each case the supposed source is later than the surah or differs on the points that matter, and where an older tradition exists, the Quran confirms its true core while correcting it.

1. P1Borrowing requires that the source existed before the borrower and that the borrower reproduces its distinctive features.
  2. P2The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated c. 629-636, but earlier material, including Jacob of Serugh's Alexander homily (d. 521), already links Alexander to the gate against Gog and Magog; the Quran omits the legend's distinctive (and fabulous) details; and the rabbinic parallels were in Hebrew and Aramaic academies far from Mecca, some compiled after Islam.
  3. ∴The parallels do not show copying. At most they show the Quran confirming true older traditions, as it says it does (5:48).

Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander Legend. The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated by most scholars to around 629-636, celebrating Heraclius' victory, while Surah al-Kahf belongs to the Meccan period. The legend makes Alexander a prophet who calls himself horned by God, has people hiding in caves from the scorching sun, names the kings of Gog and Magog, and describes a gate with iron nails. None of this is in the Quran. The Quran never names him Alexander, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "I do not know whether Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet or not" (al-Hakim; Sahih al-Jami'). 'Ali explained the name "the two-horned" as referring to blows he received on both sides of his head, not literal horns (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba). Pre-Islamic Arab poets already knew a Dhul-Qarnayn (Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari). The Bible itself praises pagan rulers as God's instruments: Cyrus is "My anointed" and "My shepherd" (Isa 44:28-45:1), and Nebuchadnezzar "My servant" (Jer 27:6).

The Sleepers of the Cave. The story of youths who fled persecution and slept for generations was told by Christians about Ephesus under Decius (c. 250), with Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) writing a homily on it. The Quran tells it with a point the Christian versions lack: people disputed their number, "three, the fourth their dog… five… seven", and "say: my Lord knows best their number" (18:22). The Quran knows the story circulates in variant forms and refuses to settle what is not important.

Abraham smashing the idols (21:51-70). Earlier Jewish texts already have Abraham attacking idols (Jubilees 12; Apocalypse of Abraham 1-8); Genesis Rabbah 38:13 (5th century) has the idols broken in his father's shop. The Quran's version is set in his people's temple and focuses on his public argument with them. Islam teaches that true accounts of the prophets can survive in Jewish tradition (the Prophet ﷺ said "narrate from the Children of Israel, there is no harm", Bukhari 3461), and the Quran confirms and corrects. Other alleged sources are later than the Quran: Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer, cited for several parallels, refers to Islam and dates to the 8th-9th century, so influence may run the other way, as Michael Pregill and Nicolai Sinai have noted.

Method. Scholars such as François de Blois and Oliver Leaman warn that in the vast literature of late antiquity, parallels are "almost too easy to find"; similarity is not a model of influence.

سَيَقُولُونَ ثَلَاثَةٌ رَّابِعُهُمْ كَلْبُهُمْ… قُل رَّبِّي أَعْلَمُ بِعِدَّتِهِم

18:22

"The Alexander Legend could have circulated orally earlier."

Possibly some motifs did, but then the Quran would be drawing on the same older tradition, not on the legend we have, and it still omits every fabulous element (the prophethood claim, the cave-dwellers, the named kings).

Your opponent says

“Surah al-Kahf copies the Syriac Alexander Legend.”

The legend is dated after 628; al-Kahf is Meccan, before 622. The Quran never calls him Alexander, never calls him a prophet (the Prophet ﷺ said he didn't know if he was one), and leaves out every fantastic detail of the legend.

The Alexander Legend postdates Surah al-Kahf and its distinctive details are absent from the Quran; the Sleepers story is told with an awareness of its variants (18:22); and some "sources" like Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer are post-Islamic.

s-history--answers-to-anachronism-charge.html: Several details critics call anachronisms (crucifixion in Pharaoh's Egypt, a "dirham" in Joseph's story, monasticism as an innovation, Pharaoh's body preserved) are either accurate or misread.

1. P1A charge of anachronism requires that the word or practice could not have existed in that setting.
  2. P2Each of these has a sound reading in its setting.
  3. ∴These are not errors.

• Crucifixion in Egypt (7:124; 20:71). The Arabic salb covers fastening or suspending a body on a stake or tree, not only the Roman cross. Genesis 40:19 has Pharaoh's baker told that Pharaoh "will hang you on a tree". Scholars of ancient execution (Samuelsson; Chapman) warn against separating crucifixion, impalement and suspension rigidly, and impalement of enemies and criminals is attested in New Kingdom Egypt.
  • "A few dirhams" (12:20). "Dirham" in 12:20 can be read as a weight of silver (Lisan al-Arab), and silver by weight (the deben) was used in Egyptian payments; critics note that the word dirham comes from Greek drachma. It is not a minted coin.
  • Monasticism "they invented" (57:27). Peter and other apostles were married (1 Cor 9:5; Mark 1:30), and the NT has no command to withdraw into celibate desert life; monasticism began with Antony of Egypt in the late 3rd century. Metzger and Ehrman note that monk-scribes even inserted "and fasting" into several verses (Mark 9:29; 1 Cor 7:5).
  • "We will preserve your body as a sign" (10:92). The Quran adds a detail the Bible lacks: Pharaoh's body would be kept as a sign. Royal mummies of the New Kingdom survive today. (The Pharaoh of the Exodus is not identified with certainty, so present this as consistent with the evidence rather than as proof.)

"Crucifixion was invented by the Persians centuries later."

The Roman form was, but the Quran's word is general, and the Bible's own Joseph story has an Egyptian king hanging a man on a tree.

Your opponent says

“The Quran has Pharaoh crucify people, but crucifixion didn't exist in Egypt.”

Salb means fastening or suspending on a stake or tree, and Genesis 40:19 has Pharaoh hang his baker "on a tree". Impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt.
Salb covers suspension on a stake, as in Genesis 40:19; the dirham is a weight of silver; monasticism began with Antony, not Jesus; and the Quran alone says Pharaoh's body would be kept as a sign.

s-history--the-splitting-of-the-moon.html: The splitting of the moon (54:1-2) is reported by many Companions through independent chains, and the Quraysh's response ("continuous magic") shows they saw something they could not deny. Its absence from other records is expected for a brief night-time event.
Use this defensively. Its strength is the mass transmission and the Quraysh's reaction, not later legends like the Kerala king.

1. P1A public event reported by many eyewitnesses through independent chains, and acknowledged by enemies, is historically credible.
  2. P2The splitting was reported by Ibn Mas'ud, Anas, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Hudhayfa, 'Ali and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, scholars classed it as mass-transmitted, and the Quran records the Quraysh calling it magic, not denying it.
  3. ∴The event is well attested.

• The Quran. "The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: continuous magic" (54:1-2). The surah was recited publicly in Mecca to the people who would have denied it if nothing had happened.
  • The reports. Bukhari and Muslim record it from several Companions; Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir (some scholars read 54:1 as eschatological). Travellers arriving in Mecca were asked and confirmed seeing it (al-Tayalisi).
  • Why not worldwide records? It was night in Arabia and day across much of the world, brief, unannounced, and most people were asleep; record-keeping of the sky was patchy (al-Khattabi, al-Qurtubi). A Kerala tradition that the Chera king Cheraman Perumal saw it and converted exists in Malabar sources, but it is late and should be treated with care.

اقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَانشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ ۝ وَإِن يَرَوْا آيَةً يُعْرِضُوا وَيَقُولُوا سِحْرٌ مُّسْتَمِرٌّ

54:1-2

Your opponent says

“If the moon split, astronomers everywhere would have recorded it.”

It was night in Arabia and day in much of the world, brief and unannounced; ancient observation was patchy. The Quraysh, who saw it, called it magic rather than deny it, and many Companions reported it independently.

Many Companions reported the moon splitting, scholars class it as mass-transmitted, and the Quraysh called it magic (54:2) rather than deny it. Its absence elsewhere is expected for a brief night event.

s-history--mecca-s-antiquity-and-the-peo.html: Critics say Mecca is unattested before Islam and that the Quran praises Trinitarian martyrs (the People of the Ditch, 85:4-8). Ancient sources point to a revered Arabian sanctuary, and the Najran martyrs' theology is disputed in the Christian sources themselves.
The pre-Islamic evidence for Mecca is suggestive rather than conclusive; Arabia is the least excavated region of the Near East. Present it as consistent evidence, not proof.

Mecca.

  • Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 3.44) describes a very holy temple among the Banizomenes of western Arabia; Gibbon read it as the Kaaba, though others dispute the location.
  • Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which some scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca; others (such as Patricia Crone) doubt it.
  • The Harran inscriptions of the Babylonian king Nabonidus (6th century BCE) name Yathrib (Medina) and Khaybar among Hijazi towns.
  • Anastasius of Sinai (7th century) mentions the Kaaba, and the Quran calls Mecca "Bakka" (3:96), echoing the "valley of Baca" of Psalm 84:6.
  • The theory that the first qibla was Petra (Dan Gibson) has been rejected by specialists, who note that the mosque orientations he relies on are imprecise.

The People of the Ditch (85:4-8). The surah praises believers burned in a trench for their faith, usually identified with the Christians of Najran killed by the Jewish king Yusuf (Dhu Nuwas) around 523. Christians argue they were Trinitarians, so the Quran praises Trinitarians. But the Christian sources disagree: the Syriac Book of the Himyarites (a damaged 12th-century manuscript) makes them Miaphysites; Chalcedonian writers claim them as Chalcedonian. Philostorgius records that the Arian missionary Theophilus the Indian converted Himyar around 354, and in the Greek Martyrdom of Arethas the persecutors ask them only to deny "the man called Jesus", not God. Ibn Abbas described them as believers in the oneness of God. The Quran praises them for believing "in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy" (85:8), and that is what it praises.

وَمَا نَقَمُوا مِنْهُمْ إِلَّا أَن يُؤْمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ

85:8

Your opponent says

“The Quran praises the Najran martyrs, who were Trinitarian Christians, so it endorses the Trinity.”

The Christian sources themselves contradict each other on their creed; an Arian mission reached Himyar in the 4th century; and the Quran praises them only for believing in Allah (85:8). Ibn Abbas called them monotheists.

Diodorus' revered Arabian temple, Ptolemy's Macoraba and Nabonidus' Hijazi towns fit an ancient Mecca. The Najran martyrs' creed is disputed in Christian sources, and the Quran praises only their faith in Allah (85:8).

s-prophecy--what-makes-a-prophecy-count.html: A prophecy is evidence only if it is specific, risky, recorded before the event, and unlikely to come true by chance. Some of the prophecies below meet these four tests; others are weaker and should be used with care.

1. P1A prediction that is vague, made after the fact, or likely anyway proves nothing.
  2. P2A prediction that is precise, against expectations, demonstrably recorded before the event, and then fulfilled cannot be explained by luck or editing.
  3. P3When a person makes many such predictions and also has a record of honesty and no worldly motive, the best explanation is that he had knowledge from God, as he claimed.
  4. ∴The test is cumulative: each fulfilled prophecy raises the probability that the Prophet ﷺ spoke from revelation.

At the Battle of the Trench (5 AH), Medina was under siege by a coalition of about 10,000. The Muslims were starving and the hypocrites were mocking them. The Prophet ﷺ struck a boulder and announced, in this order:

  1. The keys of Syria (its red palaces).
  2. The keys of Persia (the white palace of al-Mada'in).
  3. The keys of Yemen. Within a generation all three came under Muslim rule: Yemen in the Prophet's lifetime, then Syria (636) and Persia (637) (Musnad Ahmad). That is a prophecy made at the worst possible moment, against every expectation.

Your opponent says

“Prophecies are vague enough to fit anything.”

That's why the test is specificity, risk, prior recording and improbability. 'Rome will defeat Persia within three to nine years', said when Rome was collapsing, is specific, risky and recorded before the event.
Judge prophecies by specificity, risk, prior recording and improbability. The cases below pass all four tests.

s-prophecy--the-romans-will-be-victoriou.html: The Quran predicted, at the low point of the Byzantine Empire, that Rome would defeat Persia within a few years. It did, against all expectation.

1. P1Around 614-615 CE, Persia had taken Damascus and Jerusalem (carrying off the "True Cross") and soon Egypt. Byzantium seemed about to collapse.
  2. P2At exactly this time, in Mecca, the Quran announced: "The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years (bid': three to nine)" (30:2-4).
  3. P3Heraclius' counter-offensive began in 622 with the victory at Issus, about eight years after the defeat of 614, which is inside the stated range of three to nine years; his further victories through 625 also fall inside it. The Persian army was finally destroyed at Nineveh in 627, which came after the range but completed the reversal. The Quran also said "on that day the believers will rejoice" (30:4), and the Muslims' own victory at Badr (624) fell in the same period.
  4. ∴A specific, unlikely prediction with a time limit was fulfilled.

Edward Gibbon wrote (Decline and Fall ch. 46) that "at the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered, no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment, since the first twelve years of Heraclius announced the approaching dissolution of the empire."

Tesei, a non-Muslim academic, accepts that the verse predicts a Roman victory. His way out is to argue it was edited after the event. That shows how precise the prediction is: the only escape is to deny it was made in time. But the surah is Meccan, the event was famous, and Quraysh would have mocked a failed prophecy. The early sources record a wager on it between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf (Tirmidhi 3194).

غُلِبَتِ الرُّومُ ۝ فِي أَدْنَى الْأَرْضِ وَهُم مِّن بَعْدِ غَلَبِهِمْ سَيَغْلِبُونَ ۝ فِي بِضْعِ سِنِينَ

30:2-4

"Bid' is vague."

It is a defined term, meaning 3 to 9 in Arabic, and the Prophet himself told Abu Bakr to extend his wager to fit it. The Byzantine victory at Issus in 622 and the victories through 625 fall inside it. Nineveh (627) came later.

"It's a lucky guess about two empires that were always at war."

The Quran did not say "one of them will win someday". It said the side that had just been crushed would win, within a few years. Gibbon's assessment above shows how unlikely that looked at the time.

Your opponent says

“Anyone could guess that one empire would eventually beat the other.”

Not 'eventually': within bid' sinin, three to nine years, at the moment Persia held Jerusalem, Egypt and was at Constantinople's gates. Gibbon wrote that no prophecy could have seemed more distant from its fulfilment. Heraclius won at Issus in 622, eight years after the fall of Jerusalem, and the war turned from there. Nineveh followed in 627.

In about 615, with Byzantium losing everything, the Quran said Rome would win within 3-9 years; Heraclius won at Issus in 622, inside that window, then through 625 and at Nineveh in 627. Some sceptical academics read the verses as a prediction of a Roman victory but argue they were edited after the event, and a variant reading of the verbs exists.

s-prophecy--the-fire-of-the-hijaz-1256-c.html: The Prophet ﷺ foretold that a fire would emerge from the land of the Hijaz that would light up the necks of camels in Busra, in Syria (Bukhari 7118, Muslim 2902). It happened in 654 AH / 1256 CE, recorded by eyewitnesses and confirmed by modern volcanology.

1. P1The prophecy is in Bukhari and Muslim, compiled in the 3rd century AH, four centuries before the event, so it cannot have been written after the fact.
  2. P2In 1256 a volcanic eruption at Harrat Rahat near Medina produced lava flows for about 52 days, and its glow was reported as far as Tayma and Busra, roughly 900+ km away.
  3. P3Harrat Rahat has had eruptions in the past few thousand years, but 1256 is its only well-documented historical eruption.
  4. ∴A specific, unlikely event foretold centuries earlier was fulfilled exactly.

• Contemporary scholars recorded it.
    • Abu Shama al-Maqdisi in Damascus received letters from Medina's judge describing earthquakes and a fire "like a city". People in Tayma wrote letters by its light.
    • Al-Qurtubi in Egypt and al-Nawawi in Syria recorded it. Al-Nawawi called the reports mutawatir (mass-transmitted).
    • Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi, who wrote after the event, repeated that its light reached Busra.

Source Imam al-Nawawi: "A fire broke out during our time in al-Madinah…"

Source Ibn Taymiyya: the fire broke out in 655 AH and its light was seen in Busra

  • Modern geology confirms it. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and the USGS record the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption. A study by El-Masry et al. ("Historical accounts of the AD 1256 eruption near Al-Madinah") reconstructs it from the Arabic eyewitness accounts.

Source Modern geological literature confirms the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption

Source Abu Shama al-Maqdisi, al-Dhayl 'ala al-Rawdatayn: an eyewitness-era chronicle of the eruption

لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَخْرُجَ نَارٌ مِنْ أَرْضِ الْحِجَازِ تُضِيءُ أَعْنَاقَ الإِبِلِ بِبُصْرَى

Bukhari 7118

"Bukhari could have been edited after 1256."

Bukhari's Sahih was transmitted in many manuscripts and through countless teachers' chains across the Muslim world centuries before 1256. Medieval scholars themselves pointed to this hadith as fulfilled in their own time, which shows it was already well known.

Your opponent says

“Volcanoes are common in Arabia; this was a lucky guess.”

The hadith specified a fire from the Hijaz whose light would reach Busra in Syria, and it was recorded in Bukhari four centuries before the 1256 eruption near Medina, whose glow eyewitnesses reported seeing in Busra.
Bukhari recorded it in the 9th century; the Harrat Rahat volcano erupted near Medina in 1256, and its glow was seen in Busra, as eyewitnesses wrote and geologists confirm.

s-prophecy--the-mongols-and-the-fall-of-.html: Authentic hadith describe a people with broad faces, small eyes and flat noses, wearing hair shoes, who would fight the Muslims and descend on a great city by the Tigris. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, a city that did not exist in the Prophet's lifetime.

1. P1Bukhari 2928 and 3590 describe the Turks/Mongols physically: "small eyes, red faces, flat noses, their faces like hammered shields, wearing shoes of hair".
  2. P2Abu Dawud 4306 (graded hasan by al-Albani) mentions a city on the Tigris with a bridge, named "Basra" in the text, which some commentators identify with Baghdad, attacked by Banu Qantura' with broad faces and small eyes, and its people splitting into three groups.
  3. P3The Mongols under Hülegü sacked Baghdad in 1258. Baghdad stood on the Tigris, had bridges and a Basra Gate, and had over a million people. It was founded in 762, more than a century after the Prophet's death.
  4. ∴A detailed description of a people and a city that did not yet exist was fulfilled.

Ibn Taymiyya, who lived through the Mongol invasions, said that anyone who had seen Genghis Khan's and Hülegü's armies could not have described them more accurately than the Prophet ﷺ did over 600 years earlier (al-Jawab al-Sahih 2/171).

Source Ibn Taymiyya: anyone who saw these Turks could not describe them better

The common narrator of Abu Dawud's report, Sa'id ibn Jumhan, died in 136 AH, before Baghdad was built in 145 AH. The report therefore predates the city it describes.

"'Turks' were known to the Arabs, so describing them is no miracle."

The point is the whole package: their appearance, their attack on a great city by the Tigris with a bridge, and the three-way split of its people. That city was built after the narrator's death.

Your opponent says

“Turks or Mongols attacking Muslims is not a precise prophecy.”

The hadith gives physical description, hair shoes, and a great city by the Tigris, and Baghdad didn't exist when it was recorded by Companions. Its sack by the Mongols in 1258 matched every element.
Small-eyed, flat-nosed invaders in hair shoes descending on a great city by the Tigris: Baghdad, which was built after the hadith's narrator died, fell to the Mongols in 1258.

s-prophecy--barefoot-shepherds-competing.html: Among the signs of the Hour, the Prophet ﷺ said "you will see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in constructing tall buildings" (Bukhari 50, Muslim 8). Bedouin Arabia, transformed by oil wealth, is now home to the world's tallest buildings.

1. P1In the 7th century and for centuries after, many Bedouin of Arabia were poor herders who lived in tents.
  2. P2The hadith says these very people would compete in tall buildings, which is a social transformation no one could have expected.
  3. P3Within a century of the oil discoveries, the Gulf states hold the tallest building on earth (the Burj Khalifa) and the Jeddah Tower is under construction to surpass it. A related report in Ibn Abi Shayba mentions buildings in Mecca surpassing its mountains, which the Abraj al-Bait towers now do.
  4. ∴A specific and improbable social prophecy has been fulfilled.
Al-Nawawi (d. 1277) said the prophecy was not yet fulfilled in his time: desert people would become rich and boast through buildings. That shows the hadith was understood literally long before oil.

وَأَنْ تَرَى الْحُفَاةَ الْعُرَاةَ الْعَالَةَ رِعَاءَ الشَّاءِ يَتَطَاوَلُونَ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ

Muslim 8

Your opponent says

“Tall buildings exist everywhere; this is not specific.”

The prophecy is about who builds them: barefoot, destitute Bedouin shepherds competing in height. That describes the Gulf's transformation from herders to the builders of the world's tallest towers within two generations.
7th-century Bedouins were the poorest of the poor; today their descendants race to build the world's tallest towers, and Mecca's towers rise above its mountains.

s-prophecy--arabia-will-return-to-meadow.html: The Prophet ﷺ said the Hour will not come until "the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers" (Muslim 157). The word translated "returns" can imply that Arabia was once green, and palaeoclimatology has found that it was.

1. P1No one in the 7th century had evidence that the Arabian deserts were once green.
  2. P2The hadith says Arabia will return (ta'ud) to meadows and rivers, so it must have been green before. Classical commentators (Ibn al-Malik al-Karmani, Muzhir al-Din al-Zaydani) read it exactly that way.
  3. P3The Palaeodeserts Project (Michael Petraglia) and earlier work (McClure, 1984) found thousands of ancient lakes and river systems, with hippo and elephant fossils, from humid phases. Satellite imagery shows parts of Arabia greening again today.
  4. ∴A claim about Arabia's past that only modern science could verify was in the hadith from the start.

Source Studies of ancient Arabian rivers and lakes: the deserts were once green

Source McClure's 1984 doctoral thesis: lakes in the Rub' al-Khali during humid periods

حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا

Muslim 157

Your opponent says

“Saying a desert will become green is just wishful thinking.”

The key word is 'return' (ta'ud): it presupposes Arabia was once green, which no one in the 7th century knew. Palaeoclimate research has found ancient lakes and rivers across the Arabian Peninsula.
"Return to meadows and rivers": the hadith assumes a green Arabia in the past, which palaeoclimatology has now found.

s-prophecy--idolatry-returns-to-dhul-kha.html: The Prophet ﷺ said the Hour would not come until the women of the tribe of Daws sway around the idol Dhul-Khalasa (Bukhari 7116), even after Islam had destroyed it. This happened by the 19th century and the idol was demolished in the 1920s.

1. P1Dhul-Khalasa was destroyed in the Prophet's lifetime, and Arabia became entirely Muslim.
