• 'Abdullah ibn Salam, a leading rabbi of the Banu Qaynuqa', tested the Prophet ﷺ with three questions known only from rabbinic lore: the first sign of the Hour, the first food of Paradise, and why a child resembles a parent. The answers matched the rabbinic traditions, such as the banquet on the Leviathan's liver (Leviticus Rabbah), so he accepted Islam (Bukhari 3329). The Jews had called him "our best and the son of our best" before he declared his faith.
  • Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, recognised the first revelation as "the Namus (angel) that came to Moses" (Bukhari 3).
  • The Negus of Abyssinia said Surah Maryam and the Gospel "come from the same lamp".
  • Jews who conceded (Tirmidhi 2733) kissed his hands and said "we bear witness you are a prophet", but would not follow him "because David prayed that his line would never lack a prophet". That blessing was conditional on obedience (Ps 132:12; 1 Kgs 9:4-7).
  • Heraclius, according to later Christian chronicles (such as Michael the Syrian, 12th century), ordered his governors to stop resisting the Arabs because of God's promise to Ishmael.

Source Heraclius' recognition of the biblical promise to Ishmael

الَّذِينَ آتَيْنَاهُمُ الْكِتَابَ يَعْرِفُونَهُ كَمَا يَعْرِفُونَ أَبْنَاءَهُمْ

2:146

Your opponent says

“If the Jews recognised him, why did most reject him?”

The Quran says many recognised him and refused out of envy (2:109). Tirmidhi 2733 records Jews who conceded his prophethood but refused because they feared their people would abandon them. Abdullah ibn Salam, a chief rabbi, tested him and converted.
A chief rabbi who tested him and converted, a Christian scholar who recognised the angel of Moses, a Christian king who saw one lamp, and Jews who conceded he was a prophet but feared their people.

s-bible-muhammad--more-passages-and-the-.html: Beyond the main texts, several passages and pre-Islamic Jewish and Christian traditions expected a ruler or prophet from Arabia. They are supporting evidence, best used together.
Each of these is debatable on its own. Present them as a pattern that adds to the stronger texts (Deuteronomy 18, Isaiah 42, the Paraclete), not as standalone proofs.

• Psalm 72. A king to whom "desert tribes bow down" (72:9), whose rule runs "from sea to sea" (72:8), who "delivers the needy when he calls" (72:12), and for whom "prayer shall be made continually" (72:15), which Muslims do in every prayer (the salat 'ala al-Nabi). Justin Martyr argued it was not about Solomon but about Christ.
  • Genesis 49:10 (Shiloh). "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples." Muslim scholars read it as the authority of prophecy and law passing from Israel to the one whom the nations obey.
  • Psalm 120:5. "Woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar… I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war." Kedar, Ishmael's son, is the ancestor of Quraysh; the forum reads it alongside Psalm 121's "the LORD will keep your going out and your coming in" and Quran 17:80 ("cause me to enter in truth and to exit in truth"), the Hijra and return.
  • The Assumption of Moses (a 1st-century CE text, surviving in a 6th-century Latin manuscript) says from Moses' death "until his advent there will be 250 times" (10:12); some read this as pointing to the 6th century CE, a speculative reading.
  • Expectation at the time. Ibn Ishaq records that a Jewish scholar from Syria, Ibn al-Hayyiban, settled near Medina before Islam and told its Jews that a prophet was about to appear there. The 8th-century Jewish apocalypse The Secrets of Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai has an angel tell the rabbi that God brings the kingdom of Ishmael to save Israel from Rome, citing Isaiah 21:7's rider on a camel. The Syriac Chronicle of Pseudo-Zachariah (536-537) records Christians awaiting a coming figure.
  • Tirmidhi 2733. Jews who conceded his prophethood said they did not follow him because David prayed that a prophet would always come from his line. That promise was conditional on obedience (Ps 132:12; 1 Kgs 9:4-7).

وَقُل رَّبِّ أَدْخِلْنِي مُدْخَلَ صِدْقٍ وَأَخْرِجْنِي مُخْرَجَ صِدْقٍ

17:80

Your opponent says

“You can read Muhammad into anything if you try hard enough.”

Each passage alone is arguable, which is why I lead with Deuteronomy 18 and Isaiah 42. But the pattern is real: Jews in Medina were expecting a prophet before he came, a Jewish apocalypse saw the kingdom of Ishmael as God's rescue, and several texts point to Arabia and Kedar.

Psalm 72's king whom desert tribes serve and for whom prayer is made continually; Shiloh; Kedar's tents in Psalm 120; the Assumption of Moses' timetable; and Jewish expectation in Medina and in the Secrets of Rabbi Shimon. Use them as a supporting pattern.

s-miracles--the-quran-s-literary-challen.html: The Quran challenged the most eloquent Arabs of its day to produce even one surah like it. They had every motive to do so and failed, and that failure is best explained by a source beyond Muhammad ﷺ.

1. P1If a person issues a public challenge that his enemies have every motive and ability to meet, and they fail, the best explanation is that the challenge really could not be met by human beings.
  2. P2The Quran repeatedly challenged its opponents to produce a book like it, then ten surahs, then one surah (17:88, 11:13, 2:23, 10:38).
  3. P3The Quraysh were masters of the Arabic language, were desperate to discredit him, and chose war, boycott and assassination attempts rather than the far cheaper option of producing a surah.
  4. P4Their own leading experts conceded that the Quran was not poetry, soothsaying (kahana) or ordinary speech.
  5. ∴The Quran's inimitability is real, and the best explanation is that it is not the speech of a man.

The challenge is narrowed step by step. First the whole Quran (17:88: "if mankind and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce the like of it, even if they helped one another"), then ten surahs (11:13), then a single surah (2:23, 10:38). The shortest surah, al-Kawthar, is three lines. The bar was set as low as it could go, and it was set in public, in the market culture of Ukaz where poets competed for prizes.

The opponents' behaviour is the evidence. The Quraysh tried bribery (offering him wealth and kingship), a three-year boycott in the valley of Abu Talib, torture of the weak Muslims, and finally a plot to kill him. A short text in Arabic would have cost them nothing. They did not produce one, and those who later tried, such as Musaylima, produced lines that became a joke in Arabic literature.

The best-known account is that of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, reported in al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi (the chain is disputed). When the Quraysh asked him what to call the Quran so that pilgrims would avoid it, he rejected each label in turn: it is not poetry, for he knew all its metres; it is not the mumbling of a soothsayer; it is not the speech of a madman. He finally settled on "magic" only because it separates a man from his family, and Surah al-Muddaththir (74:18-25) records exactly this deliberation: "he thought and deliberated… then he said: this is nothing but magic handed down". The verse was recited publicly while al-Walid was alive and he did not deny it.

Its effect on Arabic itself confirms its status. Arabic grammar (Sibawayh), rhetoric (balagha, al-Jurjani's Dala'il al-I'jaz) and lexicography were built around the Quran as the highest standard of the language. Western scholarship notes the same: the Legacy of Islam (p. 321) describes the Quran as the standard for Arabic grammar and literary theory.

وَإِن كُنتُمْ فِي رَيْبٍ مِّمَّا نَزَّلْنَا عَلَىٰ عَبْدِنَا فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِّن مِّثْلِهِ وَادْعُوا شُهَدَاءَكُم مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ إِن كُنتُمْ صَادِقِينَ

2:23

قُل لَّئِنِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الْإِنسُ وَالْجِنُّ عَلَىٰ أَن يَأْتُوا بِمِثْلِ هَٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ لَا يَأْتُونَ بِمِثْلِهِ وَلَوْ كَانَ بَعْضُهُمْ لِبَعْضٍ ظَهِيرًا

17:88

أَفَلَا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ الْقُرْآنَ ۚ وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِندِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا

4:82

"Literary quality is subjective. Shakespeare is inimitable too."

The challenge is not "write something beautiful". It is to produce a text of the same kind, and the Quran's form is unique: it is neither poetry (shi'r, with metre) nor rhymed prose (saj'), yet it uses rhythm and rhyme throughout. The judges were not modern readers but the Arabs who knew the forms best, and they agreed it fitted none of them. Also, Shakespeare never staked his credibility on the claim that no one could match him, and his contemporaries were not trying to destroy him by matching him.

"Maybe people did meet it and Muslims destroyed the evidence."

The attempts that exist (Musaylima, Ibn al-Muqaffa' as alleged, al-Mutanabbi as rumoured) are preserved and recorded by Muslims themselves. A successful imitation would have been the single most useful weapon for the Quraysh, the apostates of the Ridda wars and the later Christian polemicists writing in Arabic, and none of them claims to have produced one.

"Non-Arabs can't judge, so the argument is useless to them."

A non-specialist can still judge the historical argument: the experts of the time, who were hostile, conceded it. That is how we accept many expert judgements we cannot check ourselves.

Your opponent says

“I could write a surah right now in rhymed Arabic. Does that disprove the Quran?”

The challenge is not rhyme. It is to match the Quran's unique form and quality, judged by people who master the language. Musaylima tried and became a byword for failure. If it were easy, the Quraysh, who had the language natively and every reason to win, would have done it rather than go to war.

The Quran set a public challenge at the lowest possible bar to the people most able and most motivated to meet it. They chose war over a few lines of Arabic, and their best critic admitted it was unlike any known form of speech.

s-miracles--the-prophet-refused-to-explo.html: On the day his son Ibrahim died, the sun was eclipsed and people said it was for Ibrahim's death. The Prophet ﷺ publicly denied it, throwing away a "sign" that would have boosted his authority. Impostors do not behave like that.

1. P1A false prophet seeks to strengthen his authority; a true prophet tells the truth even when a falsehood would help him.
  2. P2When the sun was eclipsed on the day his son died, the people attributed it to his grief, a ready-made miracle. The Prophet ﷺ immediately corrected them: "The sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or life of anyone; they are two signs among the signs of Allah" (Bukhari 1043).
  3. ∴His behaviour fits a sincere prophet and does not fit an impostor.

The event is historically anchored. Ibrahim, the Prophet's son by Mariya, died in 10 AH, and the eclipse of 27 January 632 CE is attested in the astronomical records; some Muslim sources place Ibrahim's death on that day, though the date of his death is disputed.

The point is psychological and historical. At this moment the Prophet ﷺ was grieving and the people were offering him, unprompted, a cosmic endorsement. A man inventing a religion for power would have stayed silent or accepted it. He instead gathered the people, led the eclipse prayer, and gave a sermon to correct the superstition.

This fits a wider pattern that even non-Muslim historians have noted. W. Montgomery Watt argued that his readiness to suffer persecution, the high character of those who followed him, and the greatness of what he achieved all make sincerity the default explanation, and that treating him as an impostor raises more problems than it solves. Other examples: the Quran rebukes him in his own recitation (80:1-10, the blind man; 9:43; 8:67), he lived poorly while ruling Arabia, and he refused kingship when Quraysh offered it.

إِنَّ الشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ لَا يَنْكَسِفَانِ لِمَوْتِ أَحَدٍ وَلَا لِحَيَاتِهِ، فَإِذَا رَأَيْتُمُوهُمَا فَادْعُوا اللَّهَ وَصَلُّوا

Bukhari 1043

"Sincerity doesn't prove truth. Many sincere people are wrong."

True, so this argument has a limited job: it removes the "liar" option. Combined with the others (the Quran's preservation and challenge, fulfilled prophecies, his knowledge of earlier scripture), the remaining options are "sincere and deluded" or "sincere and true". A deluded man does not produce a coherent law, a disciplined state and a book his enemies cannot match within 23 years.

"Maybe the story was invented to make him look humble."

The report is in Bukhari and Muslim through several Companions, and the eclipse is astronomically confirmed on the right day. Inventing a story in which he declines a miracle is an odd strategy for a community that collected miracle reports eagerly.

Your opponent says

“Your prophet benefited enormously from his claims: power, wives, wealth. Isn't that the profile of an impostor?”

He refused kingship and wealth when Quraysh offered them to stop preaching, died with his armour pawned to a Jew for barley, and corrected the people when an eclipse could have served him. Power came after 13 years of persecution, not before; someone seeking it would have taken the deal in Mecca.

The eclipse on the day his son died handed him a free miracle, and he publicly refused it. Alongside the Quran's self-rebukes and his refusal of worldly offers, this makes sincerity the starting point for any honest evaluation.

s-miracles--prohibitions-vindicated-alco.html: The Quran's total ban on intoxicants (5:90-91) anticipated what modern public health now concludes: there is no safe level of alcohol, and its social costs are enormous.

1. P1A law code reflects divine wisdom if it identifies a harm correctly and legislates the effective remedy, especially if the remedy was not obvious at the time.
  2. P27th-century Arabia drank heavily and wine was central to its poetry; the Quran nevertheless banned it gradually and then completely, and named its harms: enmity, hatred, and turning people from remembrance and prayer (5:91).
  3. P3Modern medicine and criminology confirm that alcohol has no safe level and drives violence, accidents and family breakdown.
  4. ∴The ban is a mark of wisdom beyond the culture it addressed.

The ban came in stages, each adapted to a society that loved wine: first noting that its harm outweighs its benefit (2:219), then forbidding prayer while intoxicated (4:43), then the final prohibition (5:90-91). The Companions poured their wine into the streets of Medina when the final verse came (Bukhari 2464).

The modern data:

  • In 2023 the WHO stated that "no level of alcohol consumption is safe" for health, since alcohol is a group 1 carcinogen.
  • In the US, about 30% of traffic deaths involve an alcohol-impaired driver (NHTSA: 11,654 deaths in 2020, cited by the CDC).
  • Alcohol is involved in roughly 40% of violent crime in US Bureau of Justice Statistics surveys (offenders who had been drinking).
  • Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders may affect up to 1 in 20 US schoolchildren (May et al., JAMA 2018).
  • Studies consistently find religiosity protects against substance abuse.

Note the Quran's diagnosis: it names social harm (enmity and hatred) before spiritual harm. That is exactly what the crime and domestic-violence numbers show.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِنَّمَا الْخَمْرُ وَالْمَيْسِرُ وَالْأَنصَابُ وَالْأَزْلَامُ رِجْسٌ مِّنْ عَمَلِ الشَّيْطَانِ فَاجْتَنِبُوهُ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ

5:90

إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَن يُوقِعَ بَيْنَكُمُ الْعَدَاوَةَ وَالْبَغْضَاءَ فِي الْخَمْرِ وَالْمَيْسِرِ وَيَصُدَّكُمْ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَعَنِ الصَّلَاةِ

5:91

"Moderate drinking is fine; some studies even say it's good for the heart."

Those studies have been widely challenged: they compared drinkers to "abstainers" who included ex-drinkers who quit because of illness, which made abstainers look sicker. Newer analyses correcting for this find no protective effect. And a law for a whole society must look at total harm, not the best-case individual.

"Prohibition failed in America, so a ban is bad policy."

US Prohibition was imposed by law on a population that did not accept it. Islam's ban is internalised as worship, and Muslim-majority societies have very low alcohol consumption as a result. The Quran's gradual method is exactly what US Prohibition lacked.

Your opponent says

“Jesus turned water into wine. Isn't it arrogant to say God bans what his prophet made?”

The Quran says earlier laws were adapted to their people and Islam completes them (5:3, 7:157). Even the Bible warns that "wine is a mocker" (Prov 20:1) and forbids it to priests on duty and Nazirites. Modern evidence that there is no safe level supports the final law, not the earlier permission.

The Quran banned alcohol in a wine-loving society, named its social harms precisely, and introduced the ban in a way people could accept. Modern data on cancer, violence, road deaths and fetal harm vindicate it.

s-miracles--zakat-and-the-economics-of-m.html: Islam built a compulsory, rule-based welfare system into worship itself, and history reports periods in which zakat is said to have nearly eliminated poverty.

1. P1A religion's law shows divine wisdom if it secures justice for the weak in a durable, practical way.
  2. P2Zakat is a fixed annual levy (2.5% on hoarded wealth above a threshold, other rates on crops and livestock) that must go to eight named categories, starting with the poor and needy (9:60). Islam also bans interest (riba), which transfers wealth from borrowers to lenders.
  3. P3Under rulers who applied it, such as Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (r. 717-720), a later source (Ibn Abd al-Hakam's Sirat Umar) reports that collectors could find no poor people to receive zakat in North Africa under him.
  4. ∴Zakat is a practical, proven system of social justice, which is what we would expect from a divine law.

Unlike voluntary charity, zakat is a pillar of Islam, as obligatory as prayer. Abu Bakr fought those who refused to pay it after the Prophet's death, which shows it was treated as a right of the poor over the rich, not a favour. The public treasury (Bayt al-Mal) also supported non-Muslims in need: Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a stipend to an old Jewish man he found begging.

T.W. Arnold's The Preaching of Islam (pp. 54, 117) records that dhimmi communities prospered under Muslim rule. The Quran also promises that charity increases rather than reduces wealth (2:261, 2:276), which fits behavioural research showing that giving increases well-being.

إِنَّمَا الصَّدَقَاتُ لِلْفُقَرَاءِ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَالْعَامِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا وَالْمُؤَلَّفَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَفِي الرِّقَابِ وَالْغَارِمِينَ وَفِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ

9:60

يَمْحَقُ اللَّهُ الرِّبَا وَيُرْبِي الصَّدَقَاتِ

2:276

"Modern welfare states do this better."

Modern states arrived at taxation-for-welfare in the 19th and 20th centuries, though earlier systems (the Torah's poor tithes, Roman grain doles, the English Poor Law of 1601) existed. Islam made it a fixed religious obligation in the 7th century, tied it to worship so it does not depend on politics, and named who must receive it. The question is not whether others later copied the idea, but where a 7th-century Arabian got it.

"The Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz report is late and idealised."

It may be idealised in detail, but the general picture of a functioning Bayt al-Mal is well documented, and the argument rests mainly on the structure of the law, not one report.

Your opponent says

“Muslim countries today are among the poorest in the world. So much for zakat.”

Most Muslim states do not apply zakat as a state system, and many run interest-based economies, so their poverty is not a test of Islamic law. Where zakat was applied systematically, sources describe poverty as nearly eliminated.
Zakat makes care for the poor a pillar of worship, with fixed rates and named recipients. Combined with the ban on interest, it is a welfare system 1,200 years ahead of the modern state.

s-miracles--the-360-joints-and-the-medic.html: Some hadith make claims about the body or medicine that are sometimes presented as scientific miracles. They are best used defensively, to show they are not absurd, rather than as primary proofs.
These arguments depend on how terms are defined and on small or preliminary studies. Don't lead with them. Use them when an opponent claims a hadith is ridiculous.

1. P1A critic who calls a hadith "obviously false" must show it contradicts established knowledge.
  2. P2The hadith of 360 joints, the fly hadith and the camel milk hadith each have plausible readings that are consistent with, or partly supported by, modern findings.
  3. ∴These hadith cannot be used as proof that the Prophet ﷺ spoke falsely.

• 360 joints (Muslim 1007). "Every human being is created with 360 joints", given as the reason each person owes a daily charity for every joint. Counts depend on what is called a joint; anatomy references give figures around 360 for synovial and other articulations, while broader counts that include all fibrous junctions reach higher (Vizniak gives about 472). The point is that 360 is a respectable count, not a guess that anatomy contradicts. Chinese and other ancient sources that mention 360 or 365 do so for calendar or cosmological reasons, and were not accessible to the Prophet ﷺ.
  • The fly hadith (Bukhari 3320). "If a fly falls into your drink, dip it fully, then remove it, for in one wing is a disease and in the other a cure." Classical scholars like al-Shashi read it as practical advice (irshad), not a command. Laboratory studies have reported antimicrobial activity in house-fly extracts and peptides (for example a 2023 review of Musca domestica antimicrobial peptides, PubMed 36619234), and some small studies report that dipping reduced bacterial counts. This is enough to show the hadith is not absurd; it is not enough to build a "miracle" on.
  • Camel milk and urine (Bukhari 233). The Prophet ﷺ prescribed these to a group of desert Arabs with a specific illness. Camel milk has documented bioactive properties. On urine, be cautious: modern health authorities warn against it because of MERS, and the hadith is about a specific remedy for specific people, not a general instruction. Yasir Qadhi and others classify much "prophetic medicine" as the Prophet's ﷺ human experience of his environment rather than revelation, citing the date-pollination hadith ("you know best the affairs of your world", Muslim 2363).
  • Ramadan fasting. Studies report benefits such as improved gut microbiome diversity, lower blood pressure, and reduced oxidative stress during Ramadan. These are good illustrations of wisdom in the law, but they are not proofs of revelation.

"Then why mention them at all?"

Because critics use them as ridicule ("Islam says dip flies in your drink"). Your goal is to neutralise the ridicule, not to win a proof.

"The Prophet's medical advice could be wrong under your own view."

Yes. Muslim scholarship distinguishes his role as a messenger from his ordinary human knowledge of agriculture or local medicine (Muslim 2363). Whether a given medical hadith is revelation is itself a scholarly question.

Your opponent says

“Your prophet told people to drink camel urine. How can anyone take that seriously?”

It was a specific remedy for a specific group in a desert setting, following practice known to the Arabs; it is not a general command. Many scholars regard such medical advice as the Prophet's experience as a man of his environment, as he said in Muslim 2363. It tells us nothing against his prophethood, any more than the Bible's medical laws do.
The 360-joint, fly and camel-milk hadith are defensible but not decisive. Use them to show critics have no real case, and build your positive case on stronger ground.

s-miracles--the-fastest-growing-religion.html: Islam's growth is real, but most of it is demographic, so use it as context, never as an argument for truth.
This is not an argument for truth. Use it only to correct someone who says Islam is dying or that its people are leaving en masse.

Pew Research Center's report on 2010-2020 found that Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group . Most of that growth comes from a young age profile and higher fertility, with switching playing a small role. Christianity, by contrast, lost more through switching than any other group.

"Popularity doesn't make something true."

Agreed, and you should say so first. Growth is a fact about people, not a proof about God.

Your opponent says

“Islam only grows because Muslims have more children.”

Correct, and I would never use growth as a proof. The arguments for Islam are the Quran's preservation, its challenge, its prophecies and the evidence for God; growth is not one of them.
Islam is the fastest-growing major religion (Pew, 2010-2020), mostly through demographics. Mention it only as context.

s-intertext--the-quran-removes-human-wea.html: Where the Bible describes God as tired, regretful or defeated, the Quran explicitly denies it, often in words that look like a direct answer to the biblical text.

1. P1A true revelation from the perfect God will not attribute weakness, ignorance or defeat to Him.
  2. P2Several biblical passages do attribute these to God, while other biblical passages contradict them, so the Bible is internally inconsistent on these points.
  3. P3The Quran consistently takes the "perfect God" side and in several places answers the problematic text directly.
  4. ∴The Quran behaves like a corrective revelation, not like a borrower.

• God "rested and was refreshed". Exodus 31:17 says that on the seventh day God "rested and was refreshed" (Hebrew wayyinnafash, literally "caught his breath"). The Quran says: "We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us" (50:38). Ayat al-Kursi adds: "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him" (2:255). The wording of 50:38 contrasts with Exodus 31:17, though it also agrees with Isaiah 40:28 and Psalm 121:4.
  • God "regretted" creating man. Genesis 6:6 says "the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart". Yet Numbers 23:19 says "God is not a man… that he should repent", and 1 Samuel 15 says both (v. 11 and 35 he regrets; v. 29 he does not). The Quran's God never regrets: His knowledge encompasses everything before it happens (57:22, 6:59).
  • God defeated by iron chariots. Judges 1:19: "the LORD was with Judah… but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain, because they had chariots of iron." The Quran: "If Allah helps you, none can overcome you" (3:160), and "Allah is never to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or the earth" (35:44).
  • God's hand "bound". Lamentations 2:3 says God "drew back His right hand", and later Jewish tradition (3 Enoch 48A; the midrash on Lamentations) describes God's right hand as held behind Him until redemption. The Quran quotes and rejects such a saying: "The Jews say: the hand of Allah is chained. Chained are their hands… rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills" (5:64).

وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامٍ وَمَا مَسَّنَا مِن لُّغُوبٍ

50:38

وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ ۚ غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَلُعِنُوا بِمَا قَالُوا ۘ بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ يُنفِقُ كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ

5:64

"These are anthropomorphisms, figures of speech. Jews and Christians don't believe God gets tired."

Then the Quran is right to say so plainly. But notice what this concedes: the biblical text, read as written, says something false about God, and only a later interpretation rescues it. The Quran does not need rescuing on these points.

"Muhammad was just a monotheist cleaning up stories he heard."

An unlettered man in Mecca would have had to know the Exodus wording about being "refreshed", the Judges verse about chariots, and an obscure rabbinic tradition about God's hand, then answer each with a precise correction. There was no Arabic Bible in his time (Metzger dates the earliest Arabic translations to the 8th or 9th century).

Your opponent says

“Your Quran also says Allah "forgets" people (9:67) and "mocks" them (2:15). Isn't that anthropomorphism too?”

Those are reciprocal expressions (mushakala): Allah "forgets" those who forgot Him means He abandons them, and the Quran itself denies literal forgetting: "My Lord neither errs nor forgets" (20:52). The Quran explains its own idiom inside the text. Exodus does not say anywhere that God never tires; it just says He rested and was refreshed.

The Bible says God was refreshed, regretted, and was stopped by chariots; other biblical passages contradict these. The Quran sides with God's perfection every time and in several places answers the text directly.

s-intertext--the-quran-restores-the-hono.html: The Bible attributes idolatry, murder and indecency to the prophets; the Quran retells the same stories and clears them. That is consistent with one source correcting another.

1. P1Prophets are God's chosen examples (6:90); a book that makes them idolaters or murderers undermines the purpose of sending them.
  2. P2The Bible says Aaron made the golden calf, Solomon worshipped idols, Moses committed premeditated murder, and Isaiah walked naked for three years.
  3. P3The Quran retells each story and removes the sin or explains it.
  4. ∴The Quran's versions preserve the logic of prophethood; the biblical versions break it.

• Aaron and the calf. Exodus 32:2-5 says Aaron collected the gold, fashioned the calf and built an altar for it. The Quran attributes the calf to "al-Samiri" and has Aaron warn the people: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90). Moses then interrogates Samiri, not Aaron (20:95-97). Aaron was the man God appointed to speak for Moses; it makes no sense that he would build the idol and keep his office.
  • Solomon and idolatry. 1 Kings 11:4-10 says Solomon's wives turned his heart to Ashtoreth and Milcom and he built shrines for them. The Quran: "Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic" (2:102).
  • Moses and the Egyptian. Exodus 2:12: Moses "looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand", a premeditated killing. The Quran: Moses struck the man in a fight to defend an Israelite and he died; Moses immediately said, "This is from the work of Satan… My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me", and he was forgiven (28:15-16). A manslaughter followed by repentance, not a murder followed by concealment.
  • Isaiah walking naked. Isaiah 20:2-3 has God command Isaiah to walk "naked and barefoot" for three years, which Muslim writers contrast with the principle "Allah does not command indecency" (7:28, in a different context).

وَلَقَدْ قَالَ لَهُمْ هَارُونُ مِن قَبْلُ يَا قَوْمِ إِنَّمَا فُتِنتُم بِهِ ۖ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَٰنُ فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي

20:90

وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ وَلَٰكِنَّ الشَّيَاطِينَ كَفَرُوا يُعَلِّمُونَ النَّاسَ السِّحْرَ

2:102

قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي فَاغْفِرْ لِي فَغَفَرَ لَهُ

28:16

"The Bible is honest about its heroes' flaws; the Quran sanitises them."

The Quran does show prophets erring and repenting: Adam (7:23), Moses (28:16), David (38:24), Jonah (21:87). What it denies is the gross sins that would make them unfit to lead: idolatry by the high priest, murder by the lawgiver, idol shrines by the temple-builder. The question is not "flaws or no flaws" but which flaws are compatible with prophethood.

"Samiri means Samaritan, and Samaritans didn't exist in Moses' time, so this is an anachronism."

Samiri is a nisba that can refer to a person, clan or place; it need not mean "Samaritan" in the later sense. Shomer/Shemer is an old Semitic name and root ("guard"). The Quran never says he was from Samaria.

Your opponent says

“If the Quran is right, why does every Bible manuscript say Aaron made the calf?”

Because the manuscripts are copies of a text that was already shaped by the time they were written; the Torah itself records its own loss and rediscovery (see the last argument in this section). And the biblical account is internally strained: Aaron is unpunished and continues as high priest while 3,000 others are killed (Exod 32:28).

The Bible makes Aaron an idol-maker, Solomon an idolater and Moses a murderer; the Quran tells the same stories while preserving their prophethood, and its versions are more coherent with the rest of the narrative.

s-intertext--the-quran-corrects-historic.html: In several stories the Quran quietly differs from the Bible on a factual detail, and in each case the Quran's version is the more plausible one.

1. P1If the Quran merely copied, its details would match its source, including the source's errors.
  2. P2In the Exodus numbers, the Garden story and Zechariah's sign, the Quran deliberately differs, and the difference resolves a problem in the biblical account.
  3. ∴The Quran is correcting, not copying.

• The size of the Exodus. Exodus 12:37 says 600,000 men on foot left Egypt, besides women and children, implying two to three million people. No archaeology supports a population that size in Sinai, and it would have outnumbered Egypt's army. The Quran has Pharaoh call them "a small band" (26:54).
  • The serpent told the truth in Genesis. In Genesis 2:17 God warns that "on the day you eat of it you will surely die"; the serpent says "you will not surely die… your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (3:4-5). Adam and Eve do not die that day, and God then says "the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil" (3:22). Read literally, the serpent seems right (a reading disputed by Jewish and Christian interpreters). In the Quran, Satan is the liar: he calls it "the tree of immortality and a kingdom that will not decay" (20:120), which is false.
  • Moses' hand. Exodus 4:6 says Moses' hand became "leprous, like snow". The Quran says it came out "white, without any harm" (20:22, 27:12, 28:32), a sign of honour rather than disease.
  • Zechariah's silence. Luke 1:20 says Zechariah was struck mute as a punishment for doubting the angel. In the Quran, Zechariah asks for a sign, and silence for three days is the sign granted (3:41, 19:10). Classical commentators such as al-Samarqandi call it a miracle, not a punishment.
  • The Israelites' words at Sinai. In Deuteronomy 5:27 the Israelites promise "we will hear and we will do" (Hebrew shama'nu ve-'asinu). The Quran reports: "they said, we hear and we disobey" (sami'na wa 'asayna, 2:93; 4:46). The Arabic sami'na wa-'asayna sounds like the Hebrew shama'nu ve-'asinu, though the roots differ ('asah vs 'asa). The Quranic phrase summarises their record after the covenant. This is a detail no one in Mecca could have constructed without knowing the Hebrew phrasing.

إِنَّ هَٰؤُلَاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ

26:54

فَوَسْوَسَ إِلَيْهِ الشَّيْطَانُ قَالَ يَا آدَمُ هَلْ أَدُلُّكَ عَلَىٰ شَجَرَةِ الْخُلْدِ وَمُلْكٍ لَّا يَبْلَىٰ

20:120

قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا

2:93

"Pharaoh calling them a small band is just his propaganda."

Possibly, but the Quran nowhere gives the 600,000 figure, and its account never requires millions. If it were copying Exodus, it would have the number.

"The Hebrew pun is a coincidence."

The phrase "we hear and…" is the covenant formula, and the Quran uses it twice in contexts about the covenant (2:93, 4:46). Commentators also note that 4:46 mentions the Jews' play on words (ra'ina), showing the Quran is aware of bilingual wordplay.

Your opponent says

“Different details just mean Muhammad heard garbled oral versions.”

Garbled versions produce random differences. These are systematic: each difference removes a problem (God being wrong in Eden, a leprous prophet, a punished priest, an impossible population). Random garbling does not repair theological and historical problems.

On the Exodus population, the Eden serpent, Moses' hand, Zechariah's sign and the Sinai covenant formula, the Quran's version fixes a problem in the biblical one. That is the pattern of a corrector, not a copyist.

s-intertext--the-quran-shows-knowledge-o.html: Where the Quran explicitly cites earlier scripture, the citation is accurate, and its themes match the earliest layers of the Jesus tradition rather than later Christian theology.

1. P1If the Quran cites a passage of the Psalms correctly and its portrait of Jesus matches the earliest reconstructed sayings source, its author had accurate knowledge of earlier revelation.
  2. P2Quran 21:105 cites Psalm 37:29 almost word for word, and the Quran's Jesus resembles the Jesus of the "Q" sayings source and the Epistle of James.
  3. ∴The Quran's relationship with earlier scripture is that of a revelation recovering what was original, as it claims (5:48).

• Psalm 37:29 in Quran 21:105. "We have written in the Psalms (al-Zabur) after the Reminder: My righteous servants shall inherit the land." Psalm 37:29: "The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell in it forever." This is the only place where the Quran explicitly quotes the Psalms by name (compare 5:45, which quotes the Torah), and the quote is exact in meaning.
  • "Lord of the worlds". The Quran's opening praise, rabb al-'alamin, matches the Jewish liturgical title ribbon kol ha-'olamim ("Master of all worlds").
  • The "Q" source. The hypothetical sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke presents Jesus as a teacher of charity, prayer and repentance who works healings, condemns the killing of the prophets (Luke 11:47-51; compare Quran 2:61, 3:21), and is accused of sorcery (Luke 11:15; compare Quran 5:110, 61:6). It has no birth narrative and no atonement theology, but it presents Jesus as the apocalyptic Son of Man, unlike the Quran.
  • The Epistle of James, from the Jerusalem church that stayed loyal to the Law, also reads like the Quran: say "if the Lord wills" before planning (James 4:13-15; Quran 18:23-24); trials refine faith (James 1:2-4; Quran 2:155); do not favour the rich (James 2:1-9; Quran 80:1-10); faith without works is dead (James 2:17-24; the Quran's constant "those who believe and do righteous deeds").
  • The Shahada pattern. Belief in God and His messenger together runs through the Bible: "they believed in the LORD and in His servant Moses" (Exod 14:31); "believe in the LORD your God… believe His prophets" (2 Chr 20:20); "this is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). The Islamic testimony of faith has the same structure.
  • Muslim writers contrast Paul's quotation of Aratus in Acts 17:28 ("we are His offspring") with the Quran's "He neither begets nor is begotten" (112:3). Paul declares all foods clean (Rom 14:14, 20); the Quran says Jesus made lawful only some of what was forbidden to the Jews (3:50).

وَلَقَدْ كَتَبْنَا فِي الزَّبُورِ مِن بَعْدِ الذِّكْرِ أَنَّ الْأَرْضَ يَرِثُهَا عِبَادِيَ الصَّالِحُونَ

21:105

وَمُصَدِّقًا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ مِنَ التَّوْرَاةِ وَلِأُحِلَّ لَكُم بَعْضَ الَّذِي حُرِّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ

3:50

"This proves Muhammad had Jewish and Christian informants."

The Quran answers the informant claim itself: "the tongue of the one they allude to is foreign, while this is clear Arabic" (16:103). The supposed informants were a foreign slave or two in Mecca, and the parallels range across Hebrew wording, rabbinic tradition, Syriac usage and early Jewish-Christian themes. No single informant had all of that, and none could have given him the Quran's style.

"Q is hypothetical."

It is the majority scholarly hypothesis for the Synoptic problem. Even setting Q aside, James gives a picture of a Law-observant community without divine-Son theology.

Your opponent says

“If the Quran knows the Bible this well, why does it get the Trinity wrong, saying Christians worship Mary (5:116)?”

5:116 does not define the Trinity as Father, Son and Mary. It asks Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides Allah, and Marian devotion did grow to include prayers and veneration directed to her (the Collyridians even offered her cakes). The Quran rejects the worship of both, which is a fair criticism of real practice.
The Quran quotes Psalm 37:29 accurately, uses Jewish liturgical language, and presents Jesus as the earliest sources do. It is consistent with its claim to recover the original message.

s-intertext--the-torah-s-own-history-rec.html: The Hebrew Bible itself says the book of the law was lost for generations, that scribes falsified it, and that many inspired books are gone, which is exactly what the Quran describes (2:79).

1. P1A book that records its own loss and its own scribes' corruption cannot claim perfect preservation.
  2. P2The Hebrew Bible records that the "book of the law" was found in the Temple under King Josiah after it had been forgotten, that the prophet Jeremiah accused the scribes of a "lying pen", and it cites about two dozen works that no longer exist.
  3. ∴By its own testimony, the Torah was not preserved in the way the Quran was, which confirms the Quran's account of the earlier scriptures.

• The book that was found. In 2 Kings 22:8 (2 Chr 34:14), the priest Hilkiah "found the book of the law" in the Temple during repairs, and King Josiah tore his clothes on hearing it because his people had not obeyed it. 2 Kings 23:22 adds that "no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges". In other words, the book of the law had been lost or neglected before Josiah's time (some scholars think it was newly composed).
  • The lying pen of the scribes. Jeremiah 8:8: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie." The Quran: "Woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say 'this is from Allah' to buy with it a small price" (2:79). Jeremiah 8:10 even adds the motive: "everyone is greedy for unjust gain".
  • Contradictions about sacrifice. Jeremiah 7:22: "I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices on the day I brought them out of Egypt"; Amos 5:25 asks, "Did you bring me sacrifices… forty years in the wilderness?" Yet Leviticus is full of sacrificial laws given in the wilderness. Jer 7:22 and Amos 5:25 have been read by some as denying that sacrifice was commanded in the wilderness.
  • Lost inspired books. The Bible cites the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Num 21:14), the Book of Jashar (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18), the chronicles of Nathan, Gad, Shemaiah and Iddo, and Solomon's 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs (1 Kgs 4:32): about two dozen works in all.
  • Ezra and the restoration. Nehemiah 8 shows Ezra reading and re-establishing the law after the Exile; the Jewish apocalypse 4 Ezra 14 even says the books were burned and Ezra rewrote them by inspiration.
  • Modern scholarship. The documentary hypothesis holds that the Torah combines several sources (J, E, D, P), visible for example in the two different orders of creation in Genesis 1 and 2 (Richard Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible?). Many scholars date Deuteronomy to Josiah's time, partly because its curses (Deut 28) follow the pattern of Esarhaddon's 7th-century vassal treaties.

فَوَيْلٌ لِّلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ الْكِتَابَ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ هَٰذَا مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ لِيَشْتَرُوا بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا

2:79

"Jeremiah 8:8 means the scribes misinterpreted the law, not that they changed the text."

The verse says the pen (Hebrew 'et, a stylus) of the scribes made it a lie, which points to writing. Ellicott's commentary takes it to refer to written work. Either way, a prophet accused the custodians of the law of falsifying it, which is the Quran's charge.

"Lost books were never meant to be scripture."

David ordered the Book of Jashar to be taught (2 Sam 1:18), and Solomon's proverbs and songs were wisdom from God by the Bible's own account. Their loss shows God did not preserve every inspired text of Israel, so "God would never let His word be lost" is not a biblical principle.

"The documentary hypothesis is disputed."

The details are, but that the Torah is composite and was edited over centuries is the mainstream view, and you do not need any particular version to make the point.

Your opponent says

“The Dead Sea Scrolls prove the Hebrew Bible was preserved.”

They show the text was fairly stable from about the 2nd century BCE, but they also contain variant forms (some closer to the Septuagint or Samaritan text), and they come centuries after Moses. Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Scrolls reads "sons of God" where the Masoretic text has "sons of Israel", a theological change.

The Bible records that the law was lost and rediscovered, that a prophet condemned the scribes' lying pen, that sacrifice laws were unknown to the prophets, and that many inspired books vanished. This matches the Quran's account in 2:79.
